Sample text:
---
# The Map of Small Distances

Marguerite Oyelaran had been mapping the town of Dunmarrow for thirty-one years, and in all that time no one had asked her why.

They asked what she was doing, of course. Children asked, and tourists on their way to somewhere better. She would tell them she was drawing a map, and they would nod and look at the paper, and she would watch them fail to understand it.

It was not a map of streets. The streets of Dunmarrow were already on every phone and on the laminated board outside the bakery. Hers was a map of small distances: how far it was from the bench by the war memorial to the exact spot where the pigeons stopped being afraid of you, and how many steps from Halloran's door to the place on the pavement where you could first smell the river. Eleven, if you were walking. Nine, if you were in a hurry and wanted it.

She had started after her husband died. The grief had no shape, and she needed something with edges. One morning she walked from her front door to the post box and counted forty-four steps. The next day she counted again and got forty-six, and the difference troubled her enough that she took out a pencil.

She learned that distance was not fixed. The walk to the post box was forty-four steps on days she felt light and forty-six on days she felt heavy. In the rain it was forty-eight, because she took shorter steps, as if the ground might be borrowed. Coming home it was never the same as going out. Coming home was always shorter, which she thought was the kindest fact she had ever discovered.

So she began to record them all, with dates and weather and a note in the margin about her mood. *Tuesday, gray, 46, thinking about his hands.* *Friday, bright, 43, nothing.* She liked the Fridays that were nothing best.

Over the years the map grew past the edge of the table and then past the edge of the spare room. It was drawn on rolls of butcher paper pinned to the walls, overlapping, cross-referenced by colored thread. Blue was distances that shrank over time. Red was distances that grew. Green was distances that stayed the same, and there were fewer of those than she would have guessed.

The distance from her house to the school, for instance, had been a steady six hundred paces for decades. Then a girl named Patience moved in next door, and it began to shorten. Patience was seven and talked constantly, and Marguerite found herself walking beside her each morning, listening to a long saga about a hamster with a criminal past. Six hundred became five hundred and eighty, then five hundred and fifty. By the end of that year it was five hundred and twenty, on the same route, in the same shoes.

Marguerite stood in her spare room and looked at that thread for a long time. It was the first time the map had told her something she didn't already know.

---

The trouble came in October, when the council announced that the old footbridge over the Marren would be replaced. The bridge was ugly and rusted and closed to bicycles. It was also, by Marguerite's records, the longest short distance in Dunmarrow. It was only ninety feet across, but people crossed it slowly. They stopped in the middle. Nobody had ever measured that, except her. Forty-one percent of the people she had watched over eleven years paused at the midpoint and looked at the water, even in the cold, even when late, even when they'd crossed it a thousand times.

The new bridge would be concrete, wide and efficient, with a railing too high to lean on.

She went to the council meeting and sat in the third row with a folder. When the chair asked for comments, she stood up and found she had no idea how to say it. "The bridge is longer than it looks," she said.

Someone coughed.

"I mean it takes people longer to cross than the length suggests. It's a place where people stop. If you build a faster one, they'll just cross it, and that will be all it is."

The chair, a kind man named Desmond who ran the hardware shop, said, "Mrs. Oyelaran, I think that's a beautiful thought. But we have to think about safety."

"Of course," she said, and sat down. Her folder felt very heavy. Inside it were eleven years of tally marks, and she saw now that they would never persuade anyone. Her whole life's work was a language spoken by one person.

---

She walked home the long way, over the old bridge. In the middle she stopped, because she always did, and looked at the brown water going by. After a while she noticed someone beside her. It was Patience, now eighteen and taller than Marguerite, home from her first term at university.

"I thought that was you," Patience said. "I heard about the meeting."

"It was foolish."

"Was it?" Patience leaned on the rail, which gave slightly, as it always had. "I stop here every time I'm home. Before the train station, before anything. I didn't know why until just now." She laughed. "Is that in your map?"

"Forty-one percent," said Marguerite.

"Am I in the forty-one?"

"You've been in it since you were eight."

Patience was quiet. Then she said, "Could I see it? The whole thing?"

No one had ever seen it. Marguerite had never offered, and no one had ever asked. She stood there with the river going by and felt something she couldn't measure in steps.

"It's a bit of a mess," she said.

"I don't mind a mess."

The walk home was two hundred and six paces, in fading light, with someone beside her. She counted them from habit and got to two hundred and one before she realized she had lost track of the numbers somewhere in the middle, listening to a story about a professor who kept bees in his office. She didn't go back and correct it. It was the first gap in thirty-one years.

---

They did build the new bridge, in the end. But that spring a plaque appeared at its center, paid for by a petition Patience organized, signed by nine hundred people. It said nothing about Marguerite. It said only: *Stop here a moment.*

People did, about forty-one percent of them. Marguerite checked.

She kept mapping until her eyes failed, and then Patience kept it for her, adding new threads in a color Marguerite had never used, a yellow-gold that stood for distances that couldn't be measured at all. There turned out to be a great many of those. The map, which had once had edges, now had none.

Marguerite thought that was correct. Coming home was always shorter than going out.
---
